report.source_text: On arrival to the ED, the patient was found to be in shock with a heart rate of 135 and a blood pressure of 74/48. Her temperature was 37 °C, she was tachypneic on her ventilator with a respiratory rate of 48 breaths per minute, saturating 100% on pulse oximetry, was pale and ill-appearing. She was unable to provide history due to tracheostomy-dependent status. The patient’s clothes and bed sheets from transport were soaked in blood. She had physical evidence of a prior left-sided craniectomy on exam and had obvious neurologic deficits including paralysis of the right body, and left-sided eye misalignment. Upon inspection of both nares, no active hemorrhage was noted, and no potential source of bleed was found either.

clinician.current_trajectory_hypothesis: 24-year-old female with remote gunshot wound to head (6 months prior) with multiple skull base fractures involving sphenoid and maxillary sinus walls now presenting with massive spontaneous right-sided epistaxis (~2 liters). report.source_text: The patient’s aneurysmal sac was accessed using an SL10 microcatheter along with 014 Synchro soft wire. ONYX embolization was performed, followed by endovascular coiling with Raymond-Roy Occlusion Classification (RROC) grade I in case the Onyx was unsuccessful (Figure 13). During the procedure, there was a daughter sac measuring 6.5 mm that was found and felt to be the point of rupture causing hemorrhage. The patient returned to baseline after reversal of anesthesia, and no operative complications were noted.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 24-year-old female with a remote gunshot wound to the head (6 months prior) complicated by multiple right-sided skull base fractures (sphenoid wall, maxillary sinus wall, medial sphenoid septum) presented to the ED with massive spontaneous right-sided epistaxis (~2 liters blood loss). On ED arrival, she was in hemorrhagic shock (BP 74/48, HR 135, RR 48) with pale, ill appearance, left eye misalignment, and right-sided paralysis. Despite massive blood loss, no active hemorrhage was visualized in the nares, suggesting a posterior/superior source. CTA of the head identified a pseudoaneurysm of the cavernous portion of the internal carotid artery. Endovascular intervention was performed using SL10 microcatheter with ONYX embolization followed by endovascular coiling (RROC grade I). A 6.5 mm daughter sac was identified as the point of rupture. The patient returned to baseline after anesthesia reversal with no operative complications.
